messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nun
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sister Teresa, a 55-year-old nun, came to treatment with a quiet but unmistakable strain that had been building for years since the day a fellow sister died unexpectedly during a ministry trip. The event had happened in a small parish house several hours from her convent, at the end of a long evening when the group had been sharing a meal and planning the next day’s work. Teresa had stepped away briefly to answer a call from another room, and when she returned, she found the sister collapsed and unresponsive. In the months that followed, Teresa kept returning to that moment with a tormenting conviction that she had not been where she should have been. She had come to believe the death happened because of the way she acted, and that she should have protected others and failed. The thought that she could not rely on herself at a critical moment became part of how she understood the loss, and it made ordinary decisions feel loaded with danger.

Those beliefs gradually shaped the way Teresa lived her days in the convent and at the parish work she still did. She began avoiding the site of the event, even when church obligations would have taken her back there, and she found excuses not to pass the room where it had happened. Anything that reminded her of someone she had lost became hard to tolerate, including old photographs, anniversary Masses, and even the sound of certain prayers that had been used at the funeral. She also started performing mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, silently repeating phrases in her mind whenever a sister left the building or when she herself had to walk alone at dusk. These habits had the feel of a desperate private duty: if she could stay away from the place, keep grief reminders at bay, and think the right words, perhaps she would never again be the one who failed to keep someone safe.

The memories themselves were not fading. Teresa described how something in her surroundings could instantly bring back the full memory without warning, and this often happened in the everyday life of the convent. The smell of strong coffee from the parish kitchen, a particular hallway light, or the sight of an empty chair at supper could catch her off guard and take her straight back to that evening. When the memory came, it was vivid and detailed: she could see the pattern of the wallpaper in the parish house, hear the scrape of a chair, and feel the sudden stillness that followed. Yet parts of the event remained blank, which disturbed her almost as much as what she remembered clearly. She would strain to reconstruct the sequence and become more convinced that something vital had been her fault. The clearer the images became, the more she felt she had missed her chance to prevent the death; the blank spaces, instead of easing her, made her distrust her own recollection and herself.

Over time, the ways she tried to manage the loss seemed to keep the memory active. Avoiding the site of the event meant that when she was unexpectedly near anything resembling it, the whole scene would rush back with even greater force. Her mental rituals, though meant to steady her, kept her attention fixed on the possibility of another catastrophe, and each silent repetition seemed to confirm that danger was always close. The more she withdrew from reminders of the sister she had lost, the more the loss itself stood out in her mind as unfinished and uncontained. Teresa found herself thinking that she had not only failed once, but had also proven she could not trust her own judgment now. That feeling deepened the sense that she should have protected others and did not deserve confidence in her own actions, which in turn made her cling more tightly to avoidance and ritual.

By the time she sought help, Teresa had become increasingly restricted in both her spiritual and practical life. She was still married to her vocation, but her world had narrowed around the fear of being caught off guard by another vivid memory or a reminder she could not bear. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was no longer able to move through her convent duties without planning around the loss, and that her mind had become as much a source of dread as the place where the death occurred. She was afraid that if she stopped her rituals, something terrible would happen again, yet she was also afraid that continuing this way would leave her forever convinced that she had failed. What she wanted most was some way to remember her sister without being seized by the scene, and some assurance that she could trust herself again.
